American lawyer and statesman, 16th president of the United States (1861–65).

Born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, Lincoln was raised on the frontier and was largely self-educated. He became a lawyer, Illinois state legislator, and U.S. representative. Angered by the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which opened the territories to slavery, he became a leader of the new [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] and reached a national audience in the 1858 Senate campaign debates against [[Stephen A. Douglas]]. He won the 1860 election as the first Republican president. A majority of the slave states then began seceding, and a month after he took office Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, starting the [[American Civil War|Civil War]].

Lincoln supervised Union strategy, including a naval blockade of Southern ports. He suspended the writ of [[Habeas corpus|habeas corpus]] in April 1861, an action that Chief Justice Roger Taney held in *Ex parte Merryman* only Congress could take; critics have viewed this and other expansions of executive power as overreach against states' rights and civil liberties. On January 1, 1863, he issued the [[Emancipation Proclamation]], declaring slaves in states "in rebellion" free; it did not immediately free those in Union border states. He delivered the [[Gettysburg Address]] on November 19, 1863, and promoted the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished chattel slavery in 1865. Re-elected in 1864, he sought to heal the nation through Reconstruction.

Five days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, he was fatally shot by [[John Wilkes Booth]] at Ford's Theatre, becoming the first U.S. president to be assassinated and leaving Vice President [[Andrew Johnson]] to manage the postwar period. He is remembered as a national hero and ranks among the greatest presidents in popular and scholarly polls.

Fully grown animal; in biology, an [[Organism|organism]] that has reached sexual maturity and is capable of reproduction.

In the human context the term carries legal and social meanings. A legal adult has attained the [[Age of majority|age of majority]] and is regarded as independent, self-sufficient, and responsible. The typical age is 18, though it varies by country. A person may be physically mature by about 15 or 16 yet not be an adult in law until 18, 20, or 21. In the United States, for example, one cannot join the armed forces or vote until 18, and one cannot take on many legal and financial responsibilities until 21. The age of majority is distinct from the minimum ages set for activities such as entering a [[Contract|contract]] or [[Marriage|marriage]]. Definitions are often inconsistent: a biologically mature person may still be treated as a child under law, and a legal adult may lack the maturity that defines an adult character.

Historically and across cultures, adulthood was determined mainly by the onset of [[Puberty|puberty]], often marked by a [[Coming of age|coming-of-age]] test or ceremony. Puberty usually begins between 10 and 12 years of age; girls typically complete it by 15–17 and boys by 16 or 17. Most modern societies now set legal adulthood by a specified age without requiring proof of preparation.

The age of full mental maturity is debated. Media claims since 2005 suggested an end point of 25, based on a brain-imaging study of participants up to age 21; more recent studies indicate that prefrontal cortex maturation continues past 30. Psychological accounts stress independence, accountability, and stable commitments, and "emerging adulthood" describes a prolonged transition in societies with extended education.

Civilization of the lower [[Nile]] River valley in northeastern Africa, a cradle of civilization that endured for over three millennia.

Ancient Egypt emerged from prehistoric Egypt around 3150 BC, by conventional chronology, when Upper and Lower Egypt were united by [[Menes]], whom most Egyptologists consider the same person as [[Narmer]]. Earlier, by about 5500 BC, small tribes in the valley had developed cultures with firm control of agriculture and animal husbandry, among them the [[Badarian culture]].

Its history unfolded as a series of stable kingdoms, the Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BC), Middle Kingdom (c. 2055–1650 BC), and New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BC), separated by Intermediate Periods of relative instability. Power peaked in the New Kingdom, which ruled much of [[Nubia]] and a considerable portion of the Levant. A slow decline followed, and Egypt was invaded or conquered by the [[Hyksos]], Kushites, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans. Its end is variously placed at 332 BC, in the Wars of Alexander the Great, or at 30 BC, when the Ptolemaic Kingdom fell to Rome. The [[Arab conquest of Egypt]] in AD 642 ended the region's Greco-Roman period.

The civilization's success rested partly on the Nile: predictable flooding and controlled irrigation produced crop surpluses that supported a dense population. A bureaucracy of scribes, religious leaders, and administrators served the reigning [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]], who in belief embodied the god Horus and upheld cosmic order.

Achievements include the techniques behind monumental pyramids, temples, and obelisks; mathematics, attested in the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus; a practical system of medicine; the first known planked boats; faience and glass technology; and the earliest known peace treaty, ratified with the Hittite Empire.

Economic system based on private ownership of the means of production and its use to obtain profit.

Its constituent elements include private property, the profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets, commodification, wage labor, and an emphasis on innovation and economic growth. Capitalist economies tend to experience [[Business cycle|business cycles]] of expansion followed by recession. Observers recognize several forms, including [[Laissez-faire|laissez-faire]], free-market, [[State capitalism|state]], and welfare capitalism, which differ in the degree of competition, regulation, and state ownership. Most economies today are mixed, combining free markets with state intervention. There is no universally agreed definition.

In its modern form capitalism emerged from agrarianism in England and from mercantilist practices in Europe between the 16th and 18th centuries. The [[Industrial Revolution]] established it as a dominant mode of production marked by factory work and a complex division of labor, a development associated with [[Adam Smith]]'s *The Wealth of Nations* (1776). Globalization spread it across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. It was largely unregulated by the state in the 19th century, became more regulated after World War II through Keynesianism, and returned toward less regulation with [[Neoliberalism|neoliberalism]] from the 1980s.

The word "capitalist", meaning an owner of capital, dates to the mid-17th century. "Capitalism" in its modern sense is attributed to Louis Blanc in 1850 and to [[Pierre-Joseph Proudhon]] in 1861; [[Karl Marx]] wrote of "capital" and the "capitalist mode of production" but not of capitalism.

Supporters credit capitalist economies with sustained growth in income, technological advance, and falling extreme poverty. Critics point to wealth disparities and recurrent business cycles, which defenders attribute to policy distortions such as subsidies rather than to markets themselves.

Chemical substance composed of identical molecules containing atoms of more than one [[Chemical element|element]] held together by [[Chemical bond|chemical bonds]].

A molecule of only one element, called a homonuclear molecule, is therefore not a compound. Because a compound has fixed proportions of two or more kinds of atoms, it can be transformed into other substances by a [[Chemical reaction|chemical reaction]], in which bonds are broken, formed, or both. Its properties differ from those of its constituent elements, and it cannot be separated into them by physical means such as filtration or distillation.

Four major types are distinguished by how the atoms are bonded: molecular compounds, held by covalent bonds; ionic compounds, by ionic bonds; intermetallic compounds, by metallic bonds; and [[Coordination complex|coordination complexes]], by coordinate covalent bonds. Examples include sodium chloride (NaCl), an ionic salt, and water and methane, which are molecular. [[Non-stoichiometric compound|Non-stoichiometric compounds]] are a disputed marginal case: their proportions are reproducible but not whole numbers, as in palladium hydride, PdHx (0.02 < x < 0.58). Many solid substances, such as many silicate minerals, lack simple formulae reflecting their bonding.

A [[Chemical formula|chemical formula]] gives the number of atoms of each element in a molecule, using standard symbols with numerical subscripts; water, with two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, is H2O. Many compounds have a unique CAS number assigned by the Chemical Abstracts Service, and more than 350,000, including mixtures, have been registered for production and use.

The term "compound", in a sense similar to the modern one, was used at least since 1661, when [[Robert Boyle]] published *The Sceptical Chymist*. In his *Logick* (1724), the English minister [[Isaac Watts]] contrasted element and compound in clear, modern terms.

Long-term pattern of [[Weather|weather]] in a region, typically averaged over 30 years.

More rigorously, climate is the mean and variability of meteorological variables, most often temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind, and precipitation, over a span from months to millions of years. In a broader sense it is the state of the [[Climate system|climate system]], which comprises the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere and the interactions among them. The word comes from the Ancient Greek *klima*, "inclination". The climate of a location is affected by its latitude, longitude, terrain, altitude, land use, and nearby water bodies and their currents. The popular phrase "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get" summarizes the distinction from weather.

The 30-year standard was defined by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), whose predecessor body designated 1901–30 as the reference period for climatological standard normals at its 1934 Wiesbaden meeting. A climate normal is the arithmetic average of a climate element over 30 years, long enough to filter out anomalies such as El Niño–Southern Oscillation but short enough to show longer trends. The 1961–90 normals serve as the baseline reference, and the next set to be published covers 1991–2020.

Some determinants of climate are nearly constant: latitude, altitude, the proportion of land to water, and proximity to oceans and mountains change only over millions of years through processes such as plate tectonics. Others are more dynamic. The [[Thermohaline circulation|thermohaline circulation]] of the ocean produces a 5 °C warming of the northern Atlantic compared with other ocean basins, other currents redistribute heat regionally, and vegetation cover affects heat absorption, water retention, and rainfall. Changes in atmospheric [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]], particularly carbon dioxide and methane, determine how much solar energy the planet retains. Climate has also fluctuated naturally over millennia through orbital variations, volcanic activity, and changes in solar output.

Climates are classified by average and typical variables, most commonly temperature and precipitation. The most widely used scheme is the [[Köppen climate classification]], first developed in 1899, which divides climates into five groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental, and polar. The Thornthwaite system, in use since 1948, adds evapotranspiration, while the Bergeron and Spatial Synoptic systems focus on the origin of air masses. Methods are broadly genetic, based on the causes of climate, or empiric, based on its effects. A common shortcoming is that they draw sharp boundaries where nature shows gradual transitions. The word originally described, in Ancient Greece, weather according to a location's latitude.

[[Paleoclimatology]] studies ancient climates. Because few direct observations exist before the 19th century, past climates are inferred from proxies: sediments in lake beds, ice cores, tree rings, pollen, and coral. [[Climate model|Climate models]] are mathematical models of past, present, and future climates. Recent warming is discussed in terms of global warming, which redistributes species; the climate scientist Lesley Ann Hughes has written that a 3 °C change in mean annual temperature corresponds to a shift in isotherms of about 300–400 km in latitude in the temperate zone, or 500 m in elevation.

Political and economic ideology aiming at a classless society based on common ownership of the means of production, with products allocated according to need.

A communist society would lack private property and social classes and ultimately money and the state. Communists disagree on the means: a libertarian socialist approach stresses workers' self-management, while a vanguardist approach uses a party-led socialist state expected to wither away. Variants include [[Anarchist communism|anarchist communism]], Marxist schools such as [[Leninism]], and religious communism. All share the analysis that capitalism divides society into the [[Proletariat|proletariat]], who sell their labor, and the [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]], who own the means of production, and that this exploitative relationship can be resolved only by social revolution.

Modern communism grew out of the socialist movement of 19th-century Europe. In 1848 [[Karl Marx]] and [[Friedrich Engels]] offered a new definition in *The Communist Manifesto*. In the 20th century, governments espousing Marxism–Leninism came to power, first in the Soviet Union through the 1917 [[Russian Revolution]], then elsewhere after World War II. For much of the century more than one-third of the world's population lived under Communist governments, characterized by one-party rule, state control of the economy and mass media, and suppression of opposition.

After the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991, many governments abolished Communist rule. Remaining Communist states include China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, and Vietnam; except for North Korea, these allow more economic competition under one-party rule. Its decline has been attributed to inefficiency, authoritarianism, and bureaucracy.

The legacy is contested. Some scholars argue that the Soviet model functioned in practice as state capitalism. Some authors cite rapid industrialization and literacy gains, while others hold communist regimes responsible for purges, forced labor, and famines; estimates of deaths remain controversial.

State of being free within society from restrictions imposed by authority on one's way of life, behavior, or political views.

In U.S. constitutional law, ordered liberty means a balanced society in which individuals may act without unnecessary interference (negative liberty) and have access to opportunities and resources (positive liberty), within a fair legal system. Liberty is sometimes distinguished from freedom: freedom is the ability to do as one wills, while liberty is the absence of arbitrary restraints, taking account of the rights of others. It can be taken away as punishment. The phrase "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness" appears in the [[United States Declaration of Independence]].

The modern idea of political liberty has roots in Greek concepts of freedom and slavery: to be free was to have no master and to live as one likes, a notion linked to democracy and described by [[Aristotle]]. In ancient India, the [[Edicts of Ashoka]] stressed tolerance in public policy. Roman law extended limited liberties to citizens only, and [[Magna Carta]] (1215) is cited as curbing royal absolutism.

[[Thomas Hobbes]] held that a free man is one not hindered from doing what he has the will and strength to do. [[John Locke]] rejected that view, arguing that in political society liberty means being under no lawmaking power except one established by consent. [[John Stuart Mill]], in *On Liberty* (1859), advanced the harm principle, limiting interference to cases of harm to others.

[[Isaiah Berlin]] framed the distinction between negative liberty, protection from tyranny and arbitrary authority, and positive liberty, self-mastery over inner compulsions such as weakness and fear. Critics of positive conceptions argue they can justify interference in the name of collective goals.

City (pop., 2011: almost 12.5 million), capital of [[Maharashtra]] state and financial capital of India.

Also known as Bombay, Mumbai lies on the Konkan coast of the Arabian Sea and has a deep natural harbour. It is the most populous city proper in India; the Mumbai Metropolitan Region exceeds 20 million. Greater Mumbai covers about 603 sq km.

Mumbai was originally an archipelago of seven islands inhabited since the South Asian Stone Age. The [[Maurya Empire]] ruled the islands from the 3rd century BC, and [[Ptolemy]] referred to them in AD 150. The deity Mumbadevi of the Koli people is believed to have given the city its name. After rule by the [[Delhi Sultanate]] and Gujarat Sultanate, the islands were ceded to the Portuguese in 1535 and transferred to the British Crown in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry; the [[East India Company]] leased them in 1668. Under the [[British Raj]], Bombay was capital of the Bombay Presidency. The Hornby Vellard land-reclamation project (1782–1845) unified the islands, and with the 19th-century cotton boom made the city a major seaport. It played a major role in the [[Indian independence movement]] and became capital of Maharashtra in 1960.

The Government of India officially changed the English name from Bombay to Mumbai in November 1995, at the insistence of the Shiv Sena party, which argued that Bombay echoed colonial rule. Some residents still use Bombay; using any other name has become controversial.

In the early 2010s the city contributed nearly 5 percent of India's GDP, one-fourth of its industrial output, and one-third of its tax revenues. It houses the Bombay High Court and Bombay Stock Exchange and is the center of Bollywood. Dense population, informal settlements, and strained infrastructure are among its challenges.

Biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life, and the science that studies it.

The intake of food provides [[Nutrient|nutrients]], divided into macronutrients, required in quantity, and micronutrients, required in trace amounts. Too much or too little of an essential nutrient can cause [[Malnutrition|malnutrition]]. Organic micronutrients are classed as [[Vitamin|vitamins]] and inorganic ones as minerals. Nitrogen, carbon, and phosphorus are the most important of the roughly 30 elements found in organic matter. Over-nutrition of macronutrients is a major cause of [[Obesity|obesity]] and raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, stroke, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, and some cancers.

The type of organism determines what it needs and how it obtains it. All forms of life require carbon, energy, and water. Animals obtain carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins by consuming other organisms; plants acquire nutrients through the soil and the atmosphere; fungi absorb them through the mycelium. [[Heterotroph|Heterotrophs]] consume the carbon of other organisms, while [[Autotroph|autotrophs]] produce nutrients from inorganic carbon such as carbon dioxide. Nutrient cycles, such as the carbon, nitrogen, and water cycles, return essential elements to the environment.

Scientific analysis of food began during the chemical revolution of the late 18th century, and modern nutrition science began in the 1910s as individual micronutrients were identified. The first vitamin chemically identified was [[Thiamine|thiamine]] in 1926, and vitamin C was identified in 1932 as a protection against [[Scurvy|scurvy]]. The first recommended dietary allowances were developed to address fears of deficiency diseases during the Great Depression and World War II.

In 2024, 150.2 million children under five were stunted and 42.8 million wasted, while 2.6 billion adults were overweight, including 940 million living with obesity.
